# Education in Sweden
Sweden's education system is structured around a compulsory nine-year comprehensive school (grundskola) for children aged approximately 6–16, divided into lower, middle, and upper stages. Prior to comprehensive school, preschool and a preschool class are available, with preschool freely offered from age three for at least three hours daily. The compulsory school curriculum mandates 16 subjects across all stages, including Swedish, mathematics, English, sciences, social studies, and arts, with national tests conducted in grades 3, 6, and 9 to ensure uniform assessment. Grading starts in year 6 with a scale from A (highest) to F (fail), and student eligibility for upper secondary education depends on passing key subjects including Swedish, English, and mathematics.
Upper secondary school (gymnasieskola) typically spans three years and offers 18 national programmes, split between preparatory tracks (focused on academic readiness for university) and vocational tracks. Students must accumulate at least 2500 course points, including core courses in language, civics, and science, and complete a diploma project to graduate. Higher education follows the Bologna Process, offering bachelor's (3 years), master's (1–2 years), and doctoral (up to 5 years) degrees, with admission requiring completion of upper secondary education or equivalent. Most university programmes are conducted in Swedish and English, and students receive financial support from the National Board of Student Aid. Independent “free schools” (friskolor) operate alongside public schools, funded by municipalities but often privately managed, and have been subjects of political debate regarding quality and equity. Sweden participates actively in international assessments like PISA and has made recent efforts to improve educational outcomes amidst challenges posed by demographic changes and immigration.
